2d29d060f941.text: Your nose does not identify an odor with a single sensor. It reads a pattern.

58e496920d1e.text: Explain why odor perception begins with volatile molecules interacting with receptors.

09b95ab11ec2.text: Describe why sparse neural representations can help distinguish similar odors.

0f41a8da6cdf.text: Airborne odorant molecules bind receptor proteins and trigger signals. The brain builds the experience of smell from this activity.

a22febe70de7.text: Many odorants are volatile chemicals, including volatile organic compounds. Not every odorant is a VOC. Molecules arrive first; perception is constructed afterward.

e74ba3834513.text: Volatility describes how readily a molecule can leave a surface or mixture and travel in air to a receptor. AeroSense later asks about food-associated airborne patterns; that is a sensing question, not a claim that every odorant is a VOC or that perception equals a molecule name.

44fa82a899df.text: A limited receptor set can still cover many odors because each odor lights a combination of receptors, and those combinations overlap. One channel is shared; the row is not.

10466b271f59.text: The matrix below uses normalized teaching values on a 0–1 scale. It is an illustrative simulation, not a biological recording.

31c69d67c100.text: The identity is encoded by the pattern, not one receptor alone.

6920308729dc.text: Combinatorial receptor coding means identity is read from which receptors are co-active. Broad tuning is expected: a receptor that responds to more than one odor is not a design failure. It is how a compact receptor family can represent a large odor space.

05a69a0e2a63.text: Similar odors can produce overlapping receptor rows. A later stage can keep only a small active subset. That sparse code does not magically name the odor. It can make neighboring patterns easier for a downstream step to tell apart.

95adcf36c279.text: Insect circuits are one biological example of this idea: receptor neurons feed the antennal lobe, then projection neurons, then mushroom-body Kenyon cells, which are typically sparsely active. The pathway in the activity is a teaching sketch, not an anatomical atlas and not AeroSense hardware.

27c7dd1da5b7.text: Sparse coding is a representation strategy, not an identification algorithm. Whether a later classifier, a Kenyon-cell-like layer, or a human reader can separate two odors still depends on the remaining differences after the transform.

2bd660dc123f.text: Choose a fictional odor and inspect six receptor channels. Add noise, compare raw, contrast-enhanced and sparse views, then compare Odor A with Odor B.

77416e242f41.text: Raw rows can overlap. Contrast can sharpen differences. Sparse views keep a small active subset. None of these steps names the odor by itself; they change how separable the pattern can be.

8a7772b4587a.text: Conceptual simulation — not experimental AeroSense data.

a7233d2f64fe.text: What does the olfactory system first detect?

7d6ad2e12995.text: Airborne chemical molecules interacting with receptors.

024c5a3a49ad.text: A finished odor name, such as “coffee,” formed before any molecule arrives.

6c5ada325ef9.text: A single exclusive receptor reserved for each familiar smell.

a970a720479e.text: Odor perception begins when airborne chemical molecules reach receptor proteins. The later experience of a named smell is constructed from receptor and circuit activity; it is not what arrives first.

4a855a9c9498.text: How can a limited number of receptors represent many odors?

3c260583a677.text: Each odor occupies one private receptor that never overlaps with any other odor.

9e12170b78d2.text: Different combinations, or patterns, of receptor activation.

0060c6fca0ac.text: Receptors wait until air temperature itself supplies an odor name.

b15743381bb0.text: Combinatorial receptor coding uses overlapping combinations. A compact receptor set can cover a large odor space because identity lives in the pattern across channels, not in a one-to-one private switch.

034990ba8a1c.text: True or false: An odor must activate exactly one receptor to be identified.

1088aafd888c.text: False. Typical odorants activate more than one receptor type, and receptor types are shared across odors. Identification, when it occurs, is recovered from the combination — and even a sparse later code is still a pattern, not a single dedicated switch.

995301d89bba.text: After seeing overlapping raw rows and a sparser view, what would you now refuse to conclude from a single receptor channel?

d7da88db9b1a.text: One odor is not one signal — it is a pattern.
